purpose: Research fixtures for calibration. Historical outcomes and gaps are evaluator-only. Orders are proposed paraphrases or reconstructions, never exact transcripts.

cases.title: Little Round Top
cases.focus: Company B, 20th Maine, on the exposed Union flank. Confederate pressure comes from the neighboring Alabama infantry.
cases.question: How far can a detached company range and still protect the line?
orders: Union: Screen the exposed flank. Take cover and use local judgment when the enemy passes.
Confederate: Advance against the Union left. Withdraw when the position becomes untenable.
cases.historical_outcome: The Union held the position. Morrill described firing from a stone wall as the Confederates fell back.
cases.model_gap: The demo models six equal starting detachments. Morrill’s actual company and its attached sharpshooters still need their own scenario data.
cases.comparison: Compare control of the high ground, the timing of flank fire and the cost to each side. Separate a matching outcome from a matching sequence.
sources: Morrill’s account • NPS landscape report, fig. 4.13

cases.title: Concord’s North Bridge
cases.focus: Captain Isaac Davis’s Acton minute company at the head of a larger provincial column, facing British light infantry at the crossing.
cases.question: When may the front company open fire?
orders: Provincial: Advance to the bridge. Hold fire until fired upon, then return fire on Buttrick’s command.
British: Guard the crossing. Fall back toward the main body if the position gives way.
cases.historical_outcome: The regulars fired, the provincials returned fire, and the regulars withdrew. Davis was killed.
cases.model_gap: Represent fire discipline, a spoken order’s reach and succession after an officer is hit. The precise source of the first British shot is uncertain.
cases.comparison: Compare first-fire sequence, who heard the command, and who controlled the crossing after the exchange.
sources: Minute Man NHP • The events of April 19
National Park Service • Captain Isaac Davis

cases.title: The north gate at Hougoumont
cases.focus: Guards defending the farm and a French assault party. The gate fight was a small action within the wider garrison defence.
cases.question: When is it worth closing the route that keeps the garrison supplied?
orders: Allied: Keep the supply entrance available. On a breach, close the leaves and hold the courtyard.
French: Reach the entrance and pass men through before the defenders can shut it.
cases.historical_outcome: A French party entered. The defenders shut the gate behind them and held the farm through the day.
cases.model_gap: A building that adds cover cannot model a working gate. Track open, contested and barred states, with men already inside.
cases.comparison: Compare gate state, entry by follow-on troops and possession of the courtyard. Vary the delay before closing.
sources: National Army Museum • Defence of Hougoumont
Age of Revolution • Closing the gates

cases.title: Pegasus Bridge
cases.focus: Major John Howard’s reinforced D Company, 2nd Ox and Bucks. The case follows the canal-bridge platoons of the wider two-bridge operation.
cases.question: Can the first platoons seize the crossing intact before the defence can react?
orders: British: Land near the canal bridge, rush the crossing and hold it intact for relief.
German: Guard the crossing, raise the alarm and organize resistance when the landing is detected.
cases.historical_outcome: The British captured the canal bridge intact. The Orne river bridge was a separate objective.
cases.model_gap: Begin at touchdown. Model platoons arriving separately, darkness, alarm delivery and the physical state of the bridge.
cases.comparison: Record when each bank is secured, whether the bridge remains passable and when headquarters learns the outcome.
sources: Airborne Assault Museum • Jim Wallwork’s account

cases.title: The ravine west of Hill 223
cases.focus: Company G, 328th U.S. Infantry. The maneuvering element is Sgt. Bernard Early’s 17-man patrol, nested in a company attack.
cases.question: Can a small patrol turn a gun position that has stopped the main advance?
orders: American: Send a patrol around the flank to reach the machine guns from the rear.
German: Keep the approach under fire. Respond locally when the patrol reaches the gun positions.
cases.historical_outcome: The patrol suffered losses, captured German troops and brought prisoners back. The outcome depended on more than one man.
cases.model_gap: Model machine-gun arcs, dead ground, local surrender and the burden of escorting captives. The precise locations and counts are debated.
cases.comparison: Compare loss of effective gunfire and return of the patrol with prisoners. Keep disputed body counts out of the pass criteria.
sources: U.S. Army History • Field study of Hill 223
U.S. Army History • The other sixteen

cases.title: The recall at Gergovia
cases.focus: Men of the Eighth Legion under centurions at the wall, against Gallic defenders. The comparison is a small sector of a much larger assault.
cases.question: What does a forward detachment do when the recall fails to reach it?
orders: Roman: Attack the outer position, then halt and retire on the recall. Each group acts on the signals it receives.
Gallic: Reinforce the threatened wall and gate. Drive back the isolated Romans.
cases.historical_outcome: Caesar says some troops continued after he sounded the recall. Defenders repulsed the attack. His account gives the Roman commander's perspective.
cases.model_gap: Model signal audibility over broken ground, formation cohesion and close combat. The engaged strength and Gallic orders are uncertain.
cases.comparison: Compare which groups receive the recall, how far they advance and whether they can withdraw together.
sources: Latin and English • VII.47, the recall
